content.text:
Assuming you mean **Kernel, the cloud browser used by Clanker: standby is a paused browser that keeps its state and stops accruing browser usage charges.**

Think of it like putting a laptop to sleep:

1. **Active:** The agent controls the browser, or you watch its Live View.
2. **Standby:** After **5 seconds with no connected clients or active control requests**, Kernel preserves the browser’s state and stops usage charges.
3. **Resume:** Reconnecting wakes the browser so work can continue. [Kernel documentation](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/browsers/standby)

**The catch:** an agent’s browser connection or an open Live View keeps it active, even when nobody is clicking. Waiting for the AI to think does not automatically mean standby.

**For Clanker:** the current code requests a **10-minute timeout**. Once standby begins, that countdown starts; if nothing reconnects, Kernel deletes the browser after the timeout. [Clanker setting](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/runtime/cloud_browser/kernel_client.py:153) · [Timeout documentation](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/browsers/termination)

**Standby preserves the current browser temporarily; timeout ends that browser session.**

content.text:
**Yes. Kernel calls these Browser Profiles:** reusable snapshots containing cookies, login sessions, local storage, open tabs, and browser preferences. [Kernel docs](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/browsers/profiles)

The flow is:

1. **Launch a browser with a profile** and `save_changes: true`.
2. **Log in normally.** The browser receives the website’s cookies.
3. **Delete the browser or let it time out.** Kernel saves its state into the profile. Disconnecting alone doesn’t save it.
4. **Launch another browser with that profile.** It loads the saved cookies and browser data. [Save behavior](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/browsers/profiles#how-profiles-work)

So **Clanker’s 10-minute browser timeout can end the browser without losing the saved login.** The website can still expire or revoke that login.

One constraint: **only one browser should write to a profile at a time**, because saving replaces the whole snapshot rather than merging changes. [Concurrency rules](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/browsers/profiles#use-profiles-concurrently)

**Clanker already has this wired into its current code:** it enables profile saving and can reuse a profile associated with the same owner’s saved login. I verified the implementation; a fresh live login-and-restore cycle hasn’t been tested here. [Browser creation](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/runtime/cloud_browser/kernel.py:282) · [Account reuse](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/runtime/cloud_browser/task_profiles.py:142)

**Profiles are isolated by user, but we use multiple task/account profiles per user, not one universal profile.**

I checked the live Kernel CLI in project `Default` and matched all **22 profiles** against Clanker’s ownership records:

| Slack user | Auth profiles | Task profiles | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `…SF7DZ` | 13 | 2 | 15 |
| `…DMWAW` | 5 | 2 | 7 |

Every profile mapped to exactly one requester. The one browser listed as active uses a task profile with **`save_changes: true`**.

What this means:

- **User isolation:** ownership is scoped by workspace, user, and execution context.
- **Cookie reuse:** Clanker must select the same saved account/profile. Logging in during one task doesn’t automatically log every other task into that account. [Profile selection](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/runtime/cloud_browser/task_profiles.py:102)

**Verified setup: user-owned profiles allocated per task/account, with explicit reuse.**

content.text:
**The extra profiles come from Clanker’s task-based allocation and incomplete cleanup. They don’t represent extra users.** My previous answer confirmed ownership but missed this problem.

The live Kernel CLI shows:

| What exists | Count |
|---|---:|
| User vaults | 3 |
| Separate credential vault | 1 |
| Profiles from failed login flows | **13** |
| Profiles Kernel marks authenticated | 5 |
| Task browsing profiles | 4 |
| **Total browser profiles** | **22** |

For example, **the same iCloud account has six profiles: five failed attempts and one successful login.**

Two things cause this:

1. **Profiles are created around tasks and account-login flows.** The profile key includes the Slack thread, so different threads can create separate profiles for the same account. Ordinary browsing can also create a task profile. This doesn’t implement your intended “three personal profiles plus one shared profile” model. [Allocation code](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/runtime/vault/managed_auth.py:642)

2. **Failed login profiles escape periodic cleanup.** Once a flow becomes `failed`, the cleanup loop stops selecting it because it only checks `pending` and `cleanup_pending`. Those profiles remain unless another cleanup path reaches them. [Cleanup code](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/runtime/vault/managed_auth.py:903)

Your **four vaults already exist**, but browser profiles aren’t mapped one-to-one to them. Reaching your four-profile model requires changing profile allocation and retiring abandoned login profiles; deleting today’s extras alone would allow them to accumulate again.
